title: The letters as letters
hook: Paul's letters are real post: greetings, travel plans, and a list of friends' names (Romans 16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shipwreck: bread broken on a storm-battered deck, and everyone safe on Malta.

When did a real letter last land in your mailbox? Paper, not email: maybe a card from a grandparent, with the news, a little advice, and a list at the end: say hi to your mom, love to the kids. A whole run of New Testament books carry Paul's name, and they aren't essays or sermons. They're letters. Real mail, sent to real people in real cities: Rome, Corinth, Philippi, Thessalonica. Somebody carried them by hand, over roads and seas, and somebody read them aloud to a room full of people who knew the sender. At the very end of Romans is a page that's easy to skip.
screen: `A REAL LETTER, ON PAPER.` → `LETTERS WITH PAUL'S NAME.` → `READ TO THE VERY END.`

segments.voice: Today's word is epistle, from the Greek for something sent. Paul's letters follow the usual letter shape of his day: who it's from, who it's to, a greeting, grace and peace, then thanks, the business, travel plans, and hellos. Romans chapter sixteen is almost all hellos. It opens, in the King James Bible: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." A note printed after Romans in the King James says the letter was sent by her. Then come more than twenty-five names. "Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus," a married couple who risked their necks for him, with a church meeting in their house. Andronicus and Junia, who were in prison with him. Tryphena and Tryphosa, who work hard. Rufus, and his mother, who was a mother to Paul too. Some he calls his kinsmen, fellow Jews; others have Greek and Latin names. Women and men, side by side. Near the end, a different voice breaks in: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord." Tertius is the scribe, writing as Paul speaks, adding his own hello. In other letters Paul takes the pen at the end and signs in his own big handwriting. In one he asks a friend to bring the coat he left behind, and his books. Why does it matter? The letters now read in church as scripture started as mail between friends. Christians read them as God's word, and they never stopped being letters, full of names.
screen: `EPISTLE: SOMETHING SENT.` · `PHOEBE CARRIES THE LETTER.` · `TWENTY-FIVE NAMES AND MORE.` · `I TERTIUS, WHO WROTE THIS.` · then, large: `NAMES MATTER.`

segments.voice: Begin one real letter or card in your head, to someone who'd be surprised to hear from you. Start the way Paul did, with a greeting, then one specific thing you're grateful for about them, some ordinary news, and a list of names to say hello to. If you pray, you can pray for each name as it comes.
Epistle. From the Greek for something sent. Paul's letters: real mail, full of travel plans, a scribe's hello, and friends' names.
Your line: names matter. Tomorrow, a one-page letter about a man who left. That's day eighty-seven.

howItsDone: In Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches, a reading from one of the New Testament letters, often called the Epistle, is read aloud at Sunday worship, the way the letters were first heard by the churches they were sent to.

original.note: Greek: a letter, something sent, from epistello, to send to. Latin epistola gave us epistle.

trapdoor: what you thought: an epistle is a holy word for a sermon.
what it means: it's a letter. Paul's were real mail, with greetings, plans, a scribe's hello and a long list of friends.
what a scholar hears: Paul's letters follow the ancient letter form, were dictated to scribes and read aloud, and Romans 16 is a rare window into who the first churches were.

notes: 'Thirteen of its twenty-seven books carry Paul's name': Hebrews is not counted. Scholars debate the authorship of several of the thirteen (e.g., the Pastorals, including 2 Timothy, cited for the coat); the script says the letters 'carry Paul's name'. Confirm.
Phoebe as the letter-carrier is a widely held inference, stated as 'very likely'.
The count of names in Romans 16 (about 26 greeted, plus others sending greetings); 'more than twenty-five' is the script's figure. Confirm.
Junia: the KJV reads Junia (a woman's name); some later readings made it masculine (Junias). The script names her without comment.
The spelling in the voice is 'Phoebe' (modern) while the quotation keeps the KJV 'Phebe'.
